blocks.text: Now we must say what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, the word by which, as we said, other Arabs rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita, in the Geography of Nubia, Clim. 1, section 1, interprets it as white weasel. Golius renders it mustela foenaria, vulgo fovina [hay-weasel, commonly called fovina], because that most learned man thought that فنك [fanak] phenec alludes to foenum [hay], and that fovina is named from foenum, whereas it takes its name from the French word for the beech. For Giggeius فنك [fanak] phenec is a certain very useful beast, from whose skin fur garments are made. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [al-fanak ḥarr ṭayyib al-rāyiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-farāʾ yujlab kathīran] [col. 1007] من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmihi ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-sammūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalī ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn lubs al-fanak]: Phenec is an animal whose skin is warm and of good odour, the most fragrant of all kinds of furs. It is brought in great quantity from Secalia. It seems to have sweet flesh. Its skin is cooler than the skin of τοῦ [tou] simor, but warmer than the skin of τοῦ [tou] sungiab. It is the custom above all for those advancing in age to be clothed in this skin. Razi: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-l-qamāqim wa-l-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī al-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa]: The skins alphenec, and alkamakim, and alhawasil are of moderate warmth, and moreover light. Damir: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwayba yūkhadh minhā al-farw qāla Ibn al-Bayṭār innahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb]: Alphenec, a small animal from which fur is taken. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and that it is brought in great quantity from the Sclavic region. This is how it should be read above, not صقالية [ṣaqāliya] Secalia (the Sclavic region, that is, the region of the Sclavs, was once in European Scythia, toward the Western Ocean, as Simocatta attests, book 6, ch. 2). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar, in the book entitled غهيد [ghhyd], that is, Explanation: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-l-sinjāb wa-l-sammūr kull dhālika sabʿ ka-l-thaʿlab wa-ibn ʿirs]: Phenec, and sungiab, and simur are all wild beasts like the fox and the weasel. So they say; from which one might gather that these skins belong to the species of marten. Yet, rather[?], الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec

[II, 417] is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls Venetian and Agricola Finnish, after the Veneti and the Finni, peoples on the Vistula in Prussia, from whom it is brought to us for use as fur. Of these peoples Ptolemy writes thus in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythōnes, eita Phinnoi]· Along the Vistula river, below the Veneti, are the Gythones, then the Finni. From these Finni, I say, the Finnish mouse seems to be named, in Arabic فنك [fanak] phenec, which the French, from its size and colour, call petigris ^{(4)}. But سنجاب [sinjāb] sungiab too is for Golius the squirrel, an animal of ash-grey colour, and its skin, with which garments are lined, or rather minium (he meant, I believe, herminium [ermine]). Damir says it is an animal in the shape of a mole, larger than a mouse, living at the tops of trees, with a bluish, very soft and very beautiful skin, in which people of refinement are clothed. It is evident that a species of squirrel is being described. Simur, too, is a kind of mouse, not entirely unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais] [col. 1008] χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας [chrōntai pros chitōnas]· Simor is the name among the Parthians of a certain species of wild mouse whose skins are used for garments. For others simur is the marten. Damir says it is an animal similar to a cat, or, in the opinion of some, النمس [al-nims] to a ferret, whose skin so excels in softness, lightness, warmth and beauty that kings and magnates are clothed in it. About both skins I could add much more, drawn from the books of the Arabs; but to explain these particulars more precisely is not a matter for our leisure, nor does it contribute much to the present subject.
Among the Greeks there is equal inconsistency in explaining the word שפן saphan.
1. There are some who render it λαγωοὺς [lagōous]; so the Vulgate translator, little hares: this we have already examined above.

2. There were some who preferred the hyena; so Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, ch. 10, where he presents Moses as saying, Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan], You shall not eat the hare, nor the hyena, that is הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what is read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē], But neither shall you eat the hare. And a little later, Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē], for which the old version has, But neither shall you eat the beast [belluam]. I would prefer beluum or belbum. For so Julius Capitolinus in Gordian III: Under Gordian there were at Rome 32 elephants, 10 elks, 10 tigers, 60 tame lions, 30 tame leopards [II, 418], 10 belbi, that is, hyenas. Yet in the Glossary Philoxenus has: Ὕαινα· ζῶον [Hyaina; zōon], bellua [beast].
